High schoolers join university walkouts in major cities and several smaller locations amid urge to fight against racism Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast They came yelling chants that “racists” weren’t “welcome here”, with signs deriding Pauline Hanson’s former fish and chip shop and the One Nation leader herself. On Thursday, thousands of students across the country put down the textbooks to walk through streets in protest against the rise of Pauline Hanson, joining the protests organised by the National Union of Students. When Kaylee, who is in Year 8 and uses they/them pronouns, had asked for the day off school, their mum had requested they lay out their reasoning. They presented her with a four-page essay.

They aren’t a political family; their mum doesn’t regularly read the news, but Kaylee said “I persuaded her” to come along. “People of a different race shouldn’t lose their rights,” Kaylee said. “And queer people have already had a lot of issues with fighting for their rights, and if that gets taken away too, that’s not okay.” Asked why they thought Hanson should not be in charge, Kaylee simply said: “I just don’t think she should be able to make those kinds of choices”. The themes from the speakers were clear - racism is not welcome here, and Hanson does not represent Australia’s youth. Former Victorian Greens leader Samantha Ratnam told the crowd she was impressed by the turnout, saying, “It gives me hope that we can stop the rise of One Nation. Everything is on the line right now.”

At one point, right-wing self-proclaimed journalist Avi Yemini turned up, surrounded by large men wearing all black and another man in a One Nation T-shirt. He tried to make his way into the crowd before being turned around by marshals. As Yemini started filming on the sidelines, a group of students ran into the background to chant “fuck Pauline Hanson”. A few meters away, a parent, Chris, said he can remember walking out of school to strike against Hanson almost 30 years ago, and now he stood with his 13-year-old daughter, Charlie. “I think that everyone should have the same rights and everyone should be able to be treated the same way,” Charlie said.
